deterministicAdjustments.originalDeltaInstruction: Show leaf fluorescence bright then collapsing in sub-second to second montage; cut to camera/PV detector readouts dropping to near-zero. Keep same tabletop/lab angle.
Show a small satellite in sunlight; indicator lights/solar panels illuminated then switch to battery icon/state. Overlay (programmatic) will later show 'hours→days' battery window.

Wide shot of PV field feeding into inverter rack; show inverter LEDs/indicators flipping to 'fault' within seconds and grid operators (control room) reacting; indicate operator timelines (minutes→hours) via later programmatic overlay.

Overlay quick-cut montage frames at the left showing darkened satellites and battery icons draining; on the right switch to a schematic n-body view where planetary dots tangle and arrows indicate possible captures, scatterings, or ejections; include a small, programmatic caption widget indicating 'N-body sensitivity — dedicated simulations needed'.

Switch sun_disk_presence to 'absent' for the visual of darkness having arrived, but keep Earth terminator and city lights subtle; overlay a simple three-icon graphic (clock→signal speed, vector→inertia, flame/thermometer→heat buffers) positioned over the night side. Do not place explicit survival-time numbers in the generated image — those belong in programmatic captions if needed.

style_spec.name: Classic 2D Documentary
style_spec.palette: Flat, readable hues — avoid neon/oversaturated color. Favor 2-4 dominant hues plus neutrals per scene so the image reads instantly, even at thumbnail size.
style_spec.shading: Restrained flat cel-shading, 1-2 tonal steps per surface (base, occasional shadow) — no painterly gradients, no hard outline on the shadow shapes themselves.
style_spec.summary: Bold 2D illustrated documentary style — thick confident outlines, rounded cartoon forms, and a restrained flat-shaded palette. Not hyper-realistic, not childish preschool cartoon, not generic corporate flat vector art.
style_spec.texture: A light, uniform paper/canvas grain overlay across the whole image — subtle enough to never read as noise or damage, present enough to avoid a flat vector-art look.
style_spec.lighting: Directional, motivated lighting with a clear implied light source and soft shadow shapes — never flat/shadowless, never harsh studio-flash lighting.
style_spec.linework: Thick, confident black outlines on every silhouette edge, with lighter interior detail lines. No sketchy cross-hatching, no photorealistic edge rendering.
style_spec.mapGrammar: Maps use a hand-illustrated cartographic style, not literally aged/parchment unless the topic calls for it. Place names and route lines are added programmatically — never baked into the image.
style_spec.perspective: Consistent one-to-two-point perspective per scene, eye-level or slightly low-angle by default for a grounded, cinematic feel.
style_spec.diagramGrammar: Diagrams use the same bold linework/palette as narrative scenes, never a generic flat corporate-infographic look. Labels and callouts are added programmatically in the video layer — never baked into the image.
style_spec.bodyProportions: Rounded, slightly simplified cartoon proportions with strong, instantly-readable silhouettes — not chibi, not hyper-stylized anime.
style_spec.faceConstruction: Expressive but simple faces — economical linework for eyes/brows/mouth, clearly readable expression. Avoid hyper-detailed photographic facial rendering and avoid oversized preschool-cartoon eyes.
style_spec.environmentDetail: Moderately detailed, readable environments and props with clear foreground/midground/background separation. Purposeful, uncluttered set-dressing — every visible object should feel intentional.
negativeConstraints: not generic corporate flat vector art

entities.canonicalSpec: The daylit hemisphere of Earth seen as a spherical globe with clear limb scattering and a distinct day–night terminator band. Surface colors: muted deep-blue oceans with visible white cloud systems (stratocumulus sheets, mid-latitude frontal clouds), pale-tan continental landmasses, and green coastal vegetation tones. Atmosphere appears as a thin graded halo around the limb (bluish near horizon fading to near-black space). The terminator is soft (not razor-sharp) and shows penumbral twilight glow extending into the night side. No exaggerated features — continents drawn at realistic scale, cloud pattern complexity moderate (no cartoon blobs). Overall scale: globe fills 40–70% of frame depending on crop; visible curvature and three-dimensional shading (subtle limb darkening on surface).
forbiddenElements: Instant global darkness or an immediately sharp shadow change on the daylit hemisphere before the ~8 min 19 s light/gravity delay
Visible change in Earth's trajectory or gravity effects before the finite light/gravity-propagation delay
Showing a bright solar corona around the Sun while the solar photosphere remains visible on the daylit globe

entities.canonicalSpec: A self-luminous stellar disk: near-circular, very bright white–yellow disk with subtle limb darkening (center slightly brighter than edge) and granulation-level texture implied by fine mottling (no photographic microdetail). Disk color leans white with mild warm (yellow) tint at lower saturations for illustration. No persistent corona visible while the photosphere is shown; when corona is illustrated it must only appear in contexts where the photosphere is blanked/occluded (eclipse-style). Scale: disk dominates its own frame region and is the primary light source in space views. Do not depict physical disappearance effects (e.g., instantaneous gravitational waves reaching Earth) before the light-time delay.
forbiddenElements: Depicting a bright, extended corona simultaneously with an unobstructed photosphere (corona-visible-only during occultation)
Showing any causal effect on Earth (illumination or gravity) before the ~499 s propagation delay

entities.canonicalSpec: A single rooftop-scale photovoltaic module: rectangular 1.6 m × 1.0 m panel with 60–72 dark blue/black monocrystalline cells in a regular grid, thin visible silver busbars and solder lines, anti-reflection glass cover with faint specular highlights, and an anodized aluminum frame (narrow profile). Backsheet and edge seal visible in cross-section shots; junction-box on rear edge with two conduit knockouts and short DC cables. Surface texture: subtle cell grain and microscopic mottling; reflections bi-directional but limited by AR coating. Scale: human-hand sized details legible when panel occupies ~15–40% of frame width.
forbiddenElements: Showing the PV panel producing useful DC current or inverter-power contribution in the absence of incident sunlight
Depicting slow, multi-minute electrical decay of PV photocurrent (PV cell current falls essentially to zero on sub-second timescales after illumination ceases)

entities.canonicalSpec: An imaging detector module shown as the rectangular sensor die inside a package or a small camera back: visible pixel grid suggested by a fine regular mosaic, microlens array implied by tiny round highlights on each pixel, and a thin color filter mosaic pattern (RGB Bayer pattern indicated abstractly, not as readable text). project.topic: What would happen if the sun disappeared

coreEntities: general relativity (finite propagation speed of gravity)
topic_model.knowledgeGap: Viewers need the detailed timeline and the physical mechanisms that determine it: why effects are delayed by light-speed propagation of gravity, how Earth's thermal inertia and atmosphere buffer temperature loss, how orbital mechanics respond when the Sun's gravity is removed, and what that implies for survival windows and long-term outcomes.
researchNeeds: Exact light-travel time and corresponding delay for gravitational changes (numerical value to present precisely).
Quantitative timescales for surface temperature decline (hours/days until freezing point, weeks/months to drop to extreme lows) based on Earth's heat capacity and radiative cooling rate.
Timescale for ocean surface to freeze and for deeper ocean freezing (typical estimates and assumptions).
How long major photosynthetic organisms (phytoplankton, crops, forests) continue to supply oxygen/food in the dark, and specific timelines for ecosystem collapse.
Behavioral/orbital calculations for Earth, Moon, and other planets once solar gravity is removed (trajectories, escape velocities, likelihood of collisions or ejections).
Survivability estimates for humans in various refuges (underground, submarines, nuclear-powered habitats) and likely thermal/electrical resource limits.
Detailed effects on satellites and space infrastructure (timelines for orbital decay or drift).
Long-term geophysical responses (mantle/core heat retention, atmospheric retention or loss over geological timescales).
topic_model.canonicalTopic: What would happen if the Sun disappeared right now?
coreMechanisms: Finite propagation speed of changes in gravity (general relativity): gravitational influence changes propagate at c, so Earth 'feels' the Sun for ~8 minutes after light goes out.
Light-travel delay: photons from the Sun take ~8 minutes to reach Earth; darkness begins after that delay.

Orbital dynamics after loss of central force: without the Sun's gravity the Earth continues in a straight (tangential) inertial path, changing the Solar System's trajectories and potentially leading to eventual ejections or new orbits.
Thermal inertia and radiative cooling: Earth's atmosphere and oceans store heat and release it over time — this controls how fast surface temperature falls (minutes→hours→days→months).

Photosynthesis shutdown and ecological collapse: loss of sunlight stops primary production, cascading through food webs on timescales from days (phytoplankton) to months/years (ecosystems, agriculture).
Phase changes in the atmosphere and oceans: condensation/freezing of atmospheric moisture and surface ocean freezing from top down, with insulation slowing complete freezing.
Human infrastructure failings without solar-driven energy inputs: power grids, agriculture, transport, and long-term habitability depend on stored or alternative energy sources.
Delayed tidal and orbital interactions (Moon/planet response): the Moon and satellites react according to local gravity changes and their own inertia, producing secondary dynamics.
topic_model.centralQuestion: If the Sun were to vanish instantly, what exactly would happen to light, gravity, Earth's climate, life, and the rest of the Solar System — and on what timescales?
topic_model.geographicScope: Solar System (Earth-focused, with sections on Moon, inner planets, outer planets, and long-term system-wide consequences)
likelyMisconceptions: The Sun's gravity would stop affecting Earth instantly.
Earth would be flung instantly into deep space or immediately freeze solid.
Darkness equals immediate zero-temperature conditions — overlooking thermal inertia and heat retention of oceans/atmosphere.
Life would vanish everywhere in minutes rather than over days/months/years in different compartments.
topic_model.viewerExpectedAnswer: A clear, time-ordered picture: nothing changes for about the light-travel delay (~8 minutes) because both light and gravitational changes travel at the speed of light; after that Earth immediately goes dark and, over minutes-to-months, loses heat according to thermal inertia (oceans/air slow the drop), photosynthesis and most life collapse within days-to-years, human survival becomes limited to well-insulated/externally powered refuges, and the Solar System's orbital structure begins to alter as gravitational influence vanishes — planets and moons move on new trajectories. The video should also correct common misconceptions (no instantaneous 'teleportation' to deep space) and show which physical mechanisms set each timescale.
topic_model.viewerPriorKnowledge: A curious viewer typically knows the Sun provides light and heat and that gravity keeps planets in orbit. Many know light takes several minutes to reach Earth and that life depends on sunlight, but they may not appreciate the details of how gravity propagates or how quickly the Earth would lose heat.

narrative_strategy.endingPayoff: A clear mental timeline and mechanism map: why the first minutes look like nothing happened; what immediate mechanical and observational effects occur; how thermal and biological systems respond across hours to years; and what longer-term orbital consequences reshape the Solar System.
narrative_strategy.centralThesis: Because changes in both light and gravity propagate at the same finite speed and because Earth's climate and biosphere have thermal and biological inertia, nothing catastrophic happens for the light-travel delay; after that, darkness and the loss of the Sun's gravitational pull trigger a cascade of mechanical, thermal, and ecological changes that play out on very different timescales from minutes to millennia.
narrative_strategy.viewerPromise: You will get a clear, time-ordered explanation that shows what changes happen when, why each timescale is set by a specific physical mechanism, and which commonly held images (instant ejection, immediate global freeze, instantaneous loss of gravity) are wrong.
plannedPayoffs: Explain that both light and changes in gravity travel at the same finite speed so there is a delay before Earth 'notices'.
Show how, after the delay, Earth goes dark instantly but keeps moving according to inertia — orbiting dynamics change into straight-line paths.

Trace the multi-timescale cooling: hours of modest drop, days to weeks of collapsing weather and freezing of surface water, months-to-years for deep freeze of ecosystems — all governed by heat capacity and insulation of oceans/atmosphere.
Lay out realistic survival windows and what infrastructure could prolong habitability.
Describe Moon and planetary dynamics qualitatively and what kinds of long-term rearrangements are plausible.
narrative_strategy.viewerQuestion: If the Sun disappeared right now, what would actually happen to light, gravity, Earth's temperature, life, and the rest of the Solar System — and on what timescales?
narrative_strategy.openingStrategy: Open on a single, cinematic image: Earth in daylight, then the disk of the Sun suddenly empty or visually 'cut out' at the center of the frame. Immediately pose the visceral questions — would we fall off into space? Would we freeze instantly? — and promise a short, ordered timeline that answers those questions by following physical mechanisms (how fast signals travel, how heat is stored and lost, and how orbits respond). The opening explicitly sets up two puzzles the episode will resolve: why nothing seems to change for a short delay, and what sequence of effects follows once the delay ends.
plannedOpenLoops: If the Sun vanished now, would Earth feel the loss immediately?
If gravity stops, do planets instantly fly away?
How fast would Earth cool and would oceans freeze solid right away?
Could humans survive and for how long?
What happens to the Moon and outer planets?

claims.narrationText: Picture yourself outside on a perfect, sunlit day — then the Sun’s disk in the sky is simply gone. Do we immediately drop off the planet? Freeze in an instant? Do the planets scatter like shrapnel? We'll follow a physical clock — seconds, minutes, hours, days, months and years — and at each tick show the mechanism that controls that timescale: the finite travel time of signals from the Sun, Earth's thermal inertia that slows cooling, and orbital inertia that governs motion once the Sun's pull no longer arrives. Those mechanisms answer the visceral questions and set up the detailed timelines we'll return to.
negativeClaims: Explosive or cinematic destruction of the Sun
Immediate visual of Earth being flung away
requiredVisualFacts: Three question captions (feel it? freeze? fly away?)
forbiddenVisualFacts: Explosive or cinematic destruction of the Sun
Immediate visual of Earth being flung away
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Show Earth in daylight, then the Sun's disk suddenly missing, and present the three visceral questions to set stakes and create curiosity.

claims.narrationText: Movies love instant, planet‑wide catastrophe — oceans leaping off Earth, people flung into space, an immediate global freeze — but the physics disagrees. The reason is concrete: light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes 19 seconds to reach us (varying by ±~9 s through the year), and changes in gravity propagate at the same finite speed. So a sudden change at the Sun cannot push or darken us until that signal arrives. The immediate aftermath is therefore calm compared with cinema: for those minutes the system keeps behaving as if nothing happened.
negativeClaims: Any footage implying instantaneous gravitational effect
requiredVisualFacts: Split-screen: movie chaos vs calm physical diagram with delay
forbiddenVisualFacts: Any footage implying instantaneous gravitational effect
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Contrast cinematic tropes (instant catastrophe) with the measured, finite delay of light and gravity to reframe expectations.

claims.narrationText: If the Sun were to vanish this instant, Earth wouldn't register it for about 499 seconds — roughly 8 minutes 19 seconds — because information (light or changes in gravity) has to travel here. Practically that means: photons already en route keep lighting our skies until that delay elapses, and the local gravitational field still reflects the Sun as it was eight minutes earlier. During those eight minutes nothing at the Sun can causally change what we see or feel here, so the planet carries on — sunlight keeps arriving and Earth continues on its orbital motion — until the trailing edge of that information finally arrives.
negativeClaims: Any depiction of instantaneous change at Earth when the Sun vanishes
requiredVisualFacts: Animation of signals traveling from Sun to Earth
forbiddenVisualFacts: Any depiction of instantaneous change at Earth when the Sun vanishes
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Show light rays and gravitational field lines propagating from the Sun to Earth with an 8:19 timer, emphasizing the causal delay.

claims.narrationText: Now fast forward eight minutes and nineteen seconds — the last photons from the Sun reach you, then stop. The first thing that happens is not a slow fade but an abrupt end to direct sunlight. That means surfaces lose the Sun’s beam and camera sensors, photovoltaic cells and the human eye's direct input all drop essentially to zero on sub‑second timescales. Electrical instruments that rely on sunlight react as fast as their electronics allow; to our senses, the sun's beam is effectively gone immediately when the last photons stop arriving.
negativeClaims: Gradual seconds-long dimming of direct sun (this is essentially instantaneous)
requiredVisualFacts: Flat shading of surfaces as direct-beam disappears
forbiddenVisualFacts: Gradual seconds-long dimming of direct sun (this is essentially instantaneous)
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Show a literal beam of sunlight cutting off, camera sensor trace and PV output falling to zero in under a second.

claims.narrationText: But even though the direct beam ends in a blink, the sky doesn't go fully black at once. The atmosphere scatters sunlight — Rayleigh scattering off molecules and Mie scattering from aerosols — so diffuse skylight persists. That gives us a twilight-like decay that can last from tens of seconds up to many minutes, and in very clear, low‑light places it can take tens of minutes before you reach true night. How long depends on where the Sun was in the sky, how dusty the air is, and local light pollution. So there’s an abrupt loss of direct sun, layered on top of a slower decay of sky brightness.
negativeClaims: Instant full darkness the moment direct-beam stops
forbiddenVisualFacts: Instant full darkness the moment direct-beam stops
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Show gradual dimming of sky brightness from daylight toward twilight over seconds-to-minutes with different skies (hazy, clear, polluted).

claims.narrationText: Inside a few seconds to a few minutes, machines and biological systems react. Grid-connected inverters and protective relays that rely on solar input typically detect a sudden loss and can trip or change modes on timescales of under a handful of seconds, which can create immediate frequency and voltage excursions on the power grid. At the same time, the tiny molecular machinery of photosynthesis shuts down extremely fast — electron transport and fluorescence signals collapse in milliseconds to seconds — while whole-leaf adjustments like stomatal movement take tens of seconds to minutes to begin responding. Those device- and plant-level timescales give us a practical short-window timeline: 0–1 s for beam loss and detector response, 1–10 s for fast electronic and biochemical transients, 10 s–1 min for twilight and early biological adjustment, and 1–10 min for short thermal and grid stabilization steps.
negativeClaims: Human-scale infrastructure failing instantly without intermediate seconds-scale effects
forbiddenVisualFacts: Human-scale infrastructure failing instantly without intermediate seconds-scale effects
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Layer a short timeline graphic while showing a PV array tripping, plant leaves closing slightly, and a twilight horizon, so viewers can feel the seconds ticking.

claims.narrationText: Planets orbit because a central force continually bends their motion; remove that force and they stop curving and coast straight. Concretely, Earth moves at ≈29.8 km/s, so in the roughly 499‑second signal delay it travels about 15,000 km along its orbit; in one hour it would traverse ≈107,000 km. When the gravitational change finally reaches Earth, the instantaneous acceleration toward the Sun vanishes and Earth's path becomes a straight-line tangent to its previous orbit at that location. That doesn't fling Earth outward in an explosion — it simply converts curved orbital motion into inertial straight-line motion at the velocity it already had.
negativeClaims: Immediate explosion or chaotic scattering at the moment signal arrives
requiredVisualFacts: Label with Earth speed ≈29.8 km/s and distance ≈15,000 km
forbiddenVisualFacts: Immediate explosion or chaotic scattering at the moment signal arrives
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Show Earth's orbit path then switch to a tangent straight-line trajectory at the moment gravity change arrives, with distance labels (≈15,000 km in ~8 min).

claims.narrationText: The Moon is close enough that short-term dynamics keep it bound to Earth. Its orbital speed (~1.02 km/s) is below the escape speed at lunar distance (~1.4 km/s), so immediately after the Sun's influence is gone the Moon stays in Earth orbit rather than flying away. Over longer timescales — centuries to millennia — the two-body interaction with Earth plus perturbations from other bodies can nudge the system into a new configuration. Those long-term possibilities (slow drift inward or outward, temporary capture, or eventual escape) are highly sensitive to small changes in geometry and timing; trustworthy answers require full N‑body simulations.
negativeClaims: A definitive long-term trajectory for the Moon
forbiddenVisualFacts: A definitive long-term trajectory for the Moon
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Show Earth and Moon remaining bound, then pull back to a chaotic N-body cloud suggesting long-term uncertainty and the need for simulations.

claims.narrationText: The instant the Sun's beam stops, Earth starts losing energy to space, but that loss is resisted by big thermal reservoirs. First, the atmosphere holds heat like a blanket: radiative cooling begins immediately but the air's heat capacity and vertical mixing mean surface temperatures fall only modestly in the first hours. Second, land surfaces release stored warmth more slowly — soils and rocks radiate and conduct heat downward over days to weeks. Third, the ocean mixed layer (the top tens of metres that exchange heat with the atmosphere) is a very large heat bank: its heat is drawn out over months to years, so coastal and sea-surface temperatures lag far behind the first atmospheric dip. Geothermal heat exists but is tiny compared to former solar input, so it cannot replace the Sun and deep cooling is ultimately inevitable. Precise regional numbers require full climate or mixed-layer model runs.
negativeClaims: Animation of the whole planet freezing solid within seconds
requiredVisualFacts: Geothermal flux labeled much smaller than solar
forbiddenVisualFacts: Animation of the whole planet freezing solid within seconds
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Layer maps and cross-sections showing atmosphere, land, and mixed-layer ocean cooling over hours, days, months with arrows indicating heat flow and insulation.

claims.narrationText: At the microscopic level photosynthesis stops almost instantly: electron transport and fluorescence collapse within milliseconds to seconds once light ends. Whole leaves and plants then begin slower adjustments — stomata respond over seconds to minutes and carbohydrate redistribution follows over hours. That means exposed crops and surface phytoplankton lose net productivity fastest (days to weeks), while large forests and soils buffer production for weeks to months. Electrically, satellites and spacecraft lose solar input immediately and switch to batteries; many small satellites can operate for hours to days before power runs out. Grid inverters and protection relays detect sudden solar loss in fractions of a second and trip or reconfigure within <1–5 s, while human operators and reserve dispatch unfold over minutes to hours. Whether communities survive beyond weeks or months depends on stored food, continuous power sources like nuclear or geothermal, and the resilience of supply chains — outcomes that need targeted engineering and logistical analysis.
negativeClaims: Definitive assertion that all humans die within a fixed short time
forbiddenVisualFacts: Definitive assertion that all humans die within a fixed short time
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Show plant leaves losing photosynthetic activity, fields wilting over days, a satellite switching to battery, and emergency power systems in a city being brought online.

claims.narrationText: Out beyond Earth, anything relying on sunlight goes dark the instant the photons stop at its location; batteries and thermal control then set how long systems limp on. On planetary scales, removing the Sun's central force leaves the system in a delicate new balance: planets, moons and asteroids still interact with one another, and those mutual tugs — not a single dominant central mass — drive the long‑term evolution. Possible outcomes include captures, scattering, or ejections and, in rare cases, collisions; which of those plays out depends strongly on the exact geometry and timing of how the Sun's influence ended. Trustworthy predictions require dedicated N‑body integrations because small differences in initial conditions amplify over time, and we don't present numerical long‑term forecasts here.
negativeClaims: A single definitive billions-of-years future trajectory
requiredVisualFacts: Schematic of planets interacting over long timescales
forbiddenVisualFacts: A single definitive billions-of-years future trajectory
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Show a montage: darkened satellites, planets drifting on new paths, and an overlay explaining that N-body simulations are needed for long-term predictions.

claims.narrationText: Here's a compact timeline to keep in your head. First: nothing changes locally for about eight minutes — then direct sunlight and solar power fall essentially to zero in under a second, though the sky fades more slowly over seconds to minutes as scattered light persists. Instruments and PV drop almost instantly, inverters/protections act in seconds and operator/reserve responses play out over minutes; photosynthesis collapses at molecular speed while whole plants and crops adjust over minutes to days. Thermally, temperatures begin falling immediately but do so over hours, days and then months because air, land and the ocean mixed layer store heat; mechanically, Earth will coast tangentally once the Sun's pull is gone and the Moon remains bound to Earth at first. The long‑term rearrangement of the Solar System — captures, escapes, collisions — is plausible but sensitive and requires N‑body modeling to predict.
negativeClaims: Any unsupported precise numeric freezing time for entire oceans
requiredVisualFacts: Layered timeline from seconds → minutes → hours → days → months → years
Mechanism labels: signal speed, inertia, thermal mass, N-body sensitivity
forbiddenVisualFacts: Any unsupported precise numeric freezing time for entire oceans
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Consolidate earlier visuals into a single layered timeline from 0 seconds to years, tying each timescale to its physical mechanism.

claims.narrationText: One last perspective: the first minutes look like almost nothing happened, and that's the point. The physics buys us that time because information can't travel faster than light. After that, darkness hits fast for direct light, machines and plants react quickly, temperatures fall more slowly because of stored heat, and orbital motion simply follows Newton's prescription once the central pull is removed. Whether communities survive for years depends on the choices and technologies we already have — batteries, continuous power sources, food reserves and resilient logistics — not on any sudden miracle. The real takeaway is a clean mental map: timescales are set by signal speed, by inertia in motion, and by heat and biological buffers. With that map you can judge for yourself what would be urgent in the first seconds, what could be managed in the first days, and what would become a long-term engineering and ecological problem.
negativeClaims: Conclusive survival time claims without caveats
forbiddenVisualFacts: Conclusive survival time claims without caveats
claims.visualCommunicationGoal: Close on a calm shot of Earth half in shadow, while overlaying the three-mechanism map and a few practical takeaways about what matters first.
